young.html: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in Geneva, a small city-republic, and became one of the most famous writers in France. He asked: Why are some people rich and others poor? Why do some rule and others obey? Was it always this way?

Rousseau imagined the very first people, living alone in the forests long ago. They needed little, were healthy and free, and felt pity when they saw others suffer. Then, little by little, people built huts, lived in families and villages, and began to compare themselves: who sings best, who is strongest, who is most admired.
Then came farming and tools of iron. One day someone put a fence around a piece of land and said, "This is mine." Rousseau said that was the start of a long road to inequality.

young.name: gb-inequality
young.cap: Step through Rousseau's story of how inequality began.

young.html: The fence game. Lay out a blanket as "the land." Put snacks on it. First, everyone shares freely. Then let one person mark off a corner with string and say "This is mine." How do the others feel? What rules would you make to keep things fair? Talk about Rousseau's question: should anyone have pulled up the stakes?

full.html: Rousseau (1712–1778) won fame with a prize essay, the Discourse on the Arts and Sciences (1750), which argued, against the spirit of his age, that the progress of the arts and sciences had not made people better. Volume 35 contains two later works: the Discourse on the Origin of Inequality (1755), written for a prize question from the Academy of Dijon, and the Discourse on Political Economy (1755), an article for Diderot's Encyclopédie.

Hobbes had said people in the state of nature would be at war, and Locke that they would already have property. Rousseau says both put into the state of nature ideas that only society gives. He asks us to set aside the facts of history and imagine "natural man": solitary, strong, with few needs, moved by two feelings, self-preservation and pity at the suffering of others, and marked by a capacity Rousseau calls perfectibility, the power to change and develop.

Two kinds of self-love. Rousseau distinguishes amour de soi, a natural care for oneself, from amour-propre, the self-love that compares itself with others and wants to be thought better. He sees amour-propre as the root of vanity, envy and much social inequality.

full.text: The first man who, having enclosed a piece of ground, bethought himself of saying This is mine, and found people simple enough to believe him, was the real founder of civil society. From how many crimes, wars and murders, from how many horrors and misfortunes might not any one have saved mankind, by pulling up the stakes, or filling up the ditch, and crying to his fellows, "Beware of listening to this impostor; you are undone if you once forget that the fruits of the earth belong to us all, and the earth itself to nobody."
full.work: Discourse on the Origin of Inequality, Part II
full.author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau

full.html: Rousseau adds at once that the idea of property depended on many earlier steps. Huts and families brought the first comparisons and the wish to be esteemed. Agriculture and metalworking divided labor and made people depend on each other. Property brought rich and poor, and conflict. Then, Rousseau says, the rich proposed a clever plan: laws and a government to keep the peace for everyone, which in fact fixed their own advantages in place. Inequality ended, in his story, in despotism.

full.cap: Rousseau's stages from the solitary savage to the first government. Notice where comparison and property enter.

full.html: Here Rousseau first sets out the idea of the general will: the will of the body politic for the common good, which should guide laws. Good government, he says, makes citizens love their country through education and fair laws, and taxes should fall more lightly on the necessities of the poor than on the luxuries of the rich.

Saying Rousseau wanted people to go back to living in forests. He says plainly that this is impossible for us. His aim was to show that much inequality is made by society, not by nature, and so might be judged and changed.

deep.html: Voltaire, sent a copy, wrote back that no one had ever used so much wit to make us want to walk on all fours. Many later thinkers took up Rousseau's question about the causes of inequality, including Adam Smith, the next rung, who reviewed the Discourse, and Marx in the next era. Critics say his state of nature is a myth with no evidence; Rousseau called it a hypothesis to help us judge the present, not a history.
Modern study of early human societies paints a more varied picture than any one 18th-century story, and scholars still debate how inequality arose with farming and settled life.

items: Is inequality natural, made by people, or both?
Does comparing ourselves with others make us better or unhappier?
Did the first fence-builder do something wrong?

questions: Rousseau said comparing ourselves to others can make us unhappy. Do you agree?
What do you think the world was like before anyone owned land?
Is it fair that some people have more than others? When is it fair, and when not?
Rousseau thought pity is natural. Do you think people are naturally kind?
If you could make one rule to keep things fair among friends, what would it be?
